Hi Jake / Sarah — following up with concrete answers + examples. Attaching a quickstart and a sample service account JSON. See notes below — I tried to keep it implementation-first so you can start the POC today.

1) Supported auth flows — recommended approach:
- Service accounts + short-lived JWTs (recommended for server-to-server): Redwood supports service accounts that are created per workspace/environment. You can mint short-lived JWTs signed by your KMS (we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM integrations) or have Redwood mint tokens if you prefer. TTLs down to 5 minutes are supported for high security use-cases.
- API keys (long-lived): supported but recommend only for internal non-sensitive tooling; rotate regularly.
- OAuth2 (3-legged): supported for user-delegated flows (rare for server-side inference but available).

2) Key rotation & zero-downtime:
- Recommended: use service account keys with rotating child keys. Redwood exposes a rotation API to create a new key, mark old key as draining (reject new requests but serve in-flight), then revoke. This allows zero-downtime swaps.
- If you manage keys externally, configure Redwood to accept JWTs signed by your key and provide the public JWK for verification; updating the JWK set is an atomic operation in our control plane.

3) RBAC & scoping:
- Roles are resource-scoped: separate roles for embeddings, generation, and administrative actions. You can attach roles to service accounts and to API keys.
- Policy rules support rate/volume limits by role and by project, so you can prevent analysts from running expensive gen jobs.

4) Routing & model selection:
- Routing can be policy-driven (recommended): you can route by header (x-redwood-route), tenant tag, or API key scope. Policies allow you to prefer cheaper quantized variants for embeddings and fallback to higher-quality models for generation.
- Example header: 
  x-redwood-route: embeddings=quantized-v1;generation=latency-v2

5) Structured output / function-calling:
- Our SDKs include a function-calling helper that validates responses against a provided JSON schema and will retry with clarified prompts if validation fails.
- For deterministic outputs, we recommend a constrained decoding strategy + schema validation in the SDK wrapper; example code in the attached quickstart shows Node and Python implementations.

6) Embeddings + reranker pipeline:
- Typical flow: embed -> store (vector DB) -> candidate retrieval -> rerank with cross-encoder or dense scorer.
- We recommend an embeddings-only role for vector generation and a separate role for reranking (which calls gen endpoints with structured output).

Attachments included:
- redwood_sdk_auth_quickstart.md (contains sample Node/Python code for service accounts, rotation, example headers for routing, and function-calling schema validation)
- sample_service_account.json (example payload with minimal perms)

Useful links:
- Auth docs: https://redwood.ai/docs/auth#service-accounts
- RBAC & policies: https://redwood.ai/docs/rbac
- POC template: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3c-redwood-acme-onboarding

If you want, I can provision a short-lived test service account for your engineering lead (Jake) that will last 2 weeks and is limited to embeddings+rerank. Let me know which environment (dev/stage) and I’ll set it up.
